abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a compositional theory of artificial life grounded in category-theoretic formalism, fundamentally reorienting how evolutionary systems are analyzed and designed. Traditional approaches to ALife modeling rely predominantly on dynamical systems theory and information-theoretic metrics, which fail to capture the relational structure across hierarchical levels of organization. We propose that artificial life emerges as a functorial mapping between a category of component-level interactions and a category of collective-level phenomena, establishing formal conditions under which genuine novelty arises. Our framework identifies a class of systems—termed compositional life—that exhibits irreducible properties not predictable from any proper subset of components, formalizing the intuitive notion of strong emergence in agent-based models. We prove that cellular automata and artificial chemistry systems satisfying the functoriality condition exhibit measurable increases in adaptive capacity over evolutionary timescales. The categorical perspective enables a unified treatment of swarm intelligence, evolutionary robotics, and synthetic biology under a single theoretical umbrella, dissolving disciplinary boundaries that have constrained ALife research. This work represents a paradigm shift from studying artificial life as a property of individual systems to understanding it as a structural relationship between organizational levels, opening new avenues for designing systems with guaranteed emergent behaviors.

Existing information-theoretic measures of self-organization in artificial life systems suffer from a fundamental limitation: they treat all correlations as equivalent regardless of their functional role in sustaining the system's viability. This paper addresses this gap by introducing Functional Information Dynamics (FID), a novel analytical framework that integrates causal relevance weighting into classical measures of emergence and self-organization. We extend the existing syntax of Φ-entropy by incorporating a intervention-based causal account that distinguishes between correlations that are merely statistical and those that actively contribute to adaptive behavior. The proposed framework decomposes total system information into three orthogonal components: structural information encoding the topology of interactions, functional information capturing causal efficacy, and contingent information representing transient statistical regularities. We validate FID against cellular automata rule spaces, demonstrating that it correctly identifies phase transitions in collective computation at substantially lower computational cost than exhaustive simulation. Furthermore, we show that FID successfully predicts the adaptive capacity of swarm systems in variable environments, outperforming existing measures by a statistically significant margin. This work significantly advances the theoretical toolkit available to ALife researchers by providing a principled method for distinguishing meaningful self-organization from spurious pattern formation.

We present Morphogenetic Collective Robotics (MCR), a radically new paradigm for constructing adaptive robotic systems in which task capabilities emerge from the self-organizing aggregation and disaggregation of functionally specialized sub-units rather than being pre-specified at the individual level. Unlike conventional evolutionary robotics approaches that optimize fixed morphologies, MCR treats the robot collective itself as a developmental system analogous to embryogenesis in biological organisms. Each module possesses limited local sensing and actuation capabilities, yet the ensemble achieves complex navigation, manipulation, and self-repair behaviors through morphogenetic gradient signaling and collective decision-making. The system architecture implements a synthetic biology-inspired genetic regulatory network on each unit, enabling context-dependent differentiation of behavioral roles—navigator, stabilizer, or propagator—without centralized control. When the collective encounters damage, surviving modules autonomously re-differentiate to compensate, demonstrating robust adaptive behavior under perturbation. Extensive simulation experiments across environments of varying complexity reveal that MCR collectives spontaneously develop non-trivial morphologies tailored to environmental demands within 50 generations of evolutionary adaptation. The paradigm establishes a new design principle in artificial life: that the most robust and adaptive systems are those whose capabilities are properties of the collective rather than the individual.

Current artificial chemistry systems struggle to reproduce the autocatalytic closure and environmental coupling that characterize biological self-maintenance, typically achieving one or the other but not both simultaneously. We introduce the Coupled Autocatalytic Reactor Network (CARN), a novel artificial chemistry platform that addresses this limitation through a two-layer architecture: an upper layer implementing molecular species competition governed by a modified hypercycle topology, and a lower layer maintaining energy gradients through compartmentalized reaction networks that mirror ATP-adenosine triphosphate dynamics. CARN differs from prior artificial chemistry implementations in three key respects: it incorporates explicit semi-permeable membrane dynamics allowing selective resource exchange, it implements a homeostatic control mechanism based on allosteric regulation principles derived from systems biology, and it integrates a coevolutionary coupling between molecular and compartmental-level selection pressures. In controlled experimental trials across 10,000 simulated time steps, CARN demonstrates sustained autocatalytic closure with robustness to environmental perturbations including nutrient scarcity, temperature fluctuation, and spurious catalysis, significantly exceeding the operational stability of existing platforms such as the Brusselator and Gray-Bott model. Importantly, CARN spontaneously evolves hierarchical organization, producing stable quasi-species that undergo fitness-driven refinement analogous to natural selection. This system provides a substantially more capable experimental platform for investigating the origins of life and the principles governing complex adaptive systems.
